title: Phlyctenular Keratoconjunctivitis (PKC): A Comprehensive Clinical Guide
summary: A localized Type IV hypersensitivity reaction of the ocular surface to microbial antigens, characterized by the formation of inflammatory nodules (phlyctenules). Historically linked to Tuberculosis, it is now most commonly associated with Staphylococcus aureus-induced blepharitis in developed nations.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Phlyctenular Keratoconjunctivitis (PKC) is a non-infectious, inflammatory nodular affection of the cornea and conjunctiva. It represents a delayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV) response to a previously sensitized endogenous microbial antigen. The hallmark is the 'phlyctenule'—a small, greyish-white nodule surrounded by a localized zone of hyperaemia, which progresses to ulceration and eventual scarring.

sections.title: Pathophysiology: The 3-Step Mechanism
content: Step 1: Sensitization — Initial exposure to microbial proteins (e.g., Staph cell wall or Tuberculoprotein) primes the T-lymphocytes.
Step 2: Re-exposure — Secondary exposure to the same antigen triggers a localized Type IV hypersensitivity reaction.
Step 3: Infiltration — Accumulation of polymorphonuclear leukocytes (early) and macrophages/lymphocytes (late) leads to subepithelial nodule formation and eventual necrosis/ulceration.

sections.title: Clinical Features & Patient Symptoms
content: Mild to severe irritation and foreign body sensation.
Intense lacrimation (tearing).
Severe Photophobia: Pathognomonic for corneal involvement; children often hide from light.
Blepharospasm: Involuntary eyelid closure.
Mucoid discharge (if secondary infection is present).
Itching (more common in Staph-related cases).

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Phlyctenule: 1-3mm hard, greyish-white elevation.
Hyperemic Zone: Fan-shaped injection pointing towards the limbus.
Fascicular Ulcer: Serpiginous-like progression across the cornea with a 'leash' of vessels.
Marginal Phlycten: Can lead to peripheral thinning and gutter formation.
Chronic Blepharitis: Scurf, collarettes, and meibomian gland dysfunction (MGD).
Salzmann Nodular Degeneration: May occur secondary to long-standing PKC.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Investigations
content: 1. Slit-Lamp Biomicroscopy: Detailed assessment of nodule morphology and corneal depth.
2. Eyelid Margin Culture: Identify Staphylococcus aureus colonization.
3. Mantoux Test (PPD) / IGRA (QuantiFERON): Essential to rule out occult TB, especially in endemic areas.
4. Chest X-Ray: Screen for pulmonary tuberculosis.
5. Sputum Analysis: If CXR is suggestive of active TB.
6. Stool Examination: Check for ova/cysts of intestinal parasites in recalcitrant pediatric cases.

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocol
content: Step 1: Topical Steroids — Loteprednol 0.5% or Fluorometholone QID (tapered slowly) to reduce inflammation.
Step 2: Antibiotic Cover — Topical Erythromycin or Bacitracin ointment for lid margins.
Step 3: Lid Hygiene — Warm compresses and lid scrubs to manage underlying Staph blepharitis.
Step 4: Systemic Treatment — Oral Doxycycline (100mg BID) or Tetracycline for adults; Oral Erythromycin for children (Rosacea-related).
Step 5: Address Underlying Cause — Anti-TB therapy (RIPE regimen) if Mantoux/CXR is positive.
Step 6: Lubrication — Preservative-free artificial tears for symptomatic relief.

sections.title: Red Flags: Immediate Concerns
content: Progressive corneal thinning or impending perforation.
Significant reduction in visual acuity.
Presence of systemic symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, chronic cough).
Steroid-induced Intraocular Pressure (IOP) spikes.
Secondary bacterial superinfection of the phlyctenular ulcer.

sections.title: Remember the Path of the Phlycten

content.explanation: S: Staph/TB (Main triggers), T: Type IV Hypersensitivity, A: Apex towards cornea, R: Rosacea association, S: Steroids (Primary treatment).

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: Photophobia in a child with a red eye should always raise suspicion for PKC or Keratitis.
The fascicular ulcer 'drags' its blood supply behind it; this leash of vessels is diagnostic.
Never start steroids without ruling out active Corneal Herpes Simplex (dendrite check).
If the phlyctenule is bilateral and recurrent, a systemic workup for TB is mandatory regardless of geographic location.
Salzmann nodules are often a long-term 'ghost' sign of previous phlyctenular disease.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Corneal Scarring: Leads to irregular astigmatism and vision loss.
Perforation: Rare, but possible in extreme thinning.
Recurrence: High if the underlying blepharitis or TB is not treated.
Secondary Infection: Bacterial keratitis can graft onto the ulcer site.
Amblyopia: In young children with central corneal scarring.

sections.title: Surgical & Advanced Interventions
content: PTK (Phototherapeutic Keratectomy): To clear superficial scars after the eye is quiet.
Lamellar Keratoplasty: Required for deep scars or significant thinning.
Penetrating Keratoplasty: Reserved for full-thickness central scars or perforation.
Gundersen Flap: In rare, non-healing recalcitrant cases.
